qualifier: This page is for media and defamation lawyers who want to move into tech law work for creators and platforms, alongside their practice.
symptom: A post goes viral, a video names someone, a channel runs a story. Then your phone rings. You send the notice, draft the reply or file the suit, and argue about words that are already out in the world.

You understand reputation, speech and content better than almost any other lawyer. You know how one careless line in a caption can turn into a year of litigation. You also know which words are safe and which ones invite a notice.
Yet the work only begins once the damage is public. The creators and brands making content every day rarely think of you until it is too late to help them cheaply.
outcome_title: Get in before the content goes out
outcome: Creators, brands and platforms run on content contracts: influencer agreements, licences, community standards and terms of use. Tech law includes all of this, and the work happens before anything is posted.

A tech law career gives you that drafting and advisory work with creators and platforms, while your media practice continues. It is the same understanding of content, used at the start of the story instead of the end. Your clients become the people producing content, not only the people hurt by it.

alternatives.why: The caseload grows, but each file is still a response to harm already done. It deepens your current practice rather than building a new career.

alternatives.t: Writing columns and commentary on media law
alternatives.why: It raises your profile among other lawyers, but creators and founders rarely read it. Visibility without a document they need seldom turns into work.
Those seats are few and usually filled through long relationships. Waiting for one leaves your skill parked for years. Meanwhile, new creators start out every day with nobody advising them.

reframe: Who owns a video, who may reuse it, what a brand can demand and what a creator can refuse are all contract terms. You already weigh these questions every time you defend a piece of content. Creators often sign brand deals without anyone checking those terms.

So the gap is positioning, not ability. Creators and platforms simply do not know that a defamation lawyer can draft their agreements. One clean influencer agreement is often enough to show them. Creators judge a lawyer by the agreement in front of them.
cost_title: If you keep waiting for the call
cost: If you stay unclear, your work keeps starting after the harm, and the growing world of creators and platforms keeps hiring other people at the stage where you could help most. That stage is still open to you.
role_h2: What tech law work looks like for a media and defamation lawyer
role: Drafting an influencer agreement. On Day 3 we draft one in five clauses: engagement and fee, deliverables, IP licence, content ownership and brand guidelines. Each clause turns a familiar dispute into a clear, agreed term.

Reviewing a platform's terms, including its community standards and IP ownership, two of the six checks in Day 3's review. You know exactly how vague standards play out once a post is challenged. Your review would flag them before the first takedown request arrives.

Advising ad-funded platforms. Day 2 explains six ways tech companies make money, including advertising, and each creates content, IP and policy work. Tech law also covers disputes over impersonation, defamation and takedowns, where your court experience counts.
first_artifact: Your first tech law document comes on Day 3: an influencer agreement drafted with us, live. With the startup terms review the same evening, you would have two samples that speak directly to creators, brands and platforms. A creator or brand manager can see at a glance how each one protects them.
longer_term: With 2 hours a day, one learning and one on outreach, six months could take you through IP and takedowns, website policies and tech contracts, all listed on the Day 2 plan. Your media practice can carry on, and each skill adds a sample you can share.

faq.q: Do creators actually need contracts drafted?
faq.a: Day 3 covers the legal work influencers need, from brand deals to content ownership. Every brand collaboration raises the questions our five-clause agreement answers.

faq.q: Can I reach creators without breaching Bar Council rules?
faq.a: Advocates cannot advertise or solicit, so we do not teach chasing briefs. Day 3 also shows how to help lawyers and founders get onto podcasts, a way to build relationships by being useful first. Check with your State Bar Council if unsure.

faq.q: Is this only for lawyers at big media firms?
faq.a: No. Any lawyer who handles content disputes already understands the questions. The camp gives you the drafting side, starting with three live evenings, 24 to 26 Oct. Media and defamation practice is a strong base for content contracts.

faq.q: Do I need technical knowledge of how platforms work?
faq.a: No coding is needed. Day 1 explains SaaS, APIs and three more concepts plainly, and the rest follows how the platform makes money.

closing_title: Media and defamation lawyers: move into tech law for creators and platforms
closing: Media and defamation lawyers already understand content, reputation and ownership. Creators and platforms need that understanding in their contracts before anything goes live. Join us for three evenings and move into tech law without pausing your practice.
